Some random, unfiltered thoughts on AI and the market:

The gulf between “San Francisco” and “New York” has never been wider than it is right now 

AI is accelerating in capability, rapidly and in a way that is structurally changing, and in many ways upending, the nature of the firm and the fundamentals of capitalism

If that sounds extreme, consider that Anthropic has ~6,000 employees, Meta has 67,000, and both companies are worth ~$1.5T

Talk to your average startup and it’s clear that, given the opportunity to start from scratch, nobody is building their companies “the old way.” 

Talk to your average Fortune 500 company and it’s clear that getting an AI agent into production at scale is a Herculean task

Intelligence may not be the bottleneck, but firms built from the foundational assumption that intelligence is improving quickly in capability and price are scaling at a genuinely unbelievably velocity

There’s a reason Zuck wanted to fire 60% of many of the teams at his company, in large part likely out of frustration that he can’t start from scratch like his competitors had the luxury of doing

A structurally weaker Nvidia and OpenAI have minimal impact on the pace and impact of AI diffusing across the economy (“San Francisco”), but completely breaks the models built in “New York.” Hence the absolute freak-out these last few weeks. It was all priced to go perfectly and now things are not perfect 

But for the boots on the ground, AI will not slow down. And counterintuitively, economic weakness might accelerate diffusion. After all, tokens are much more fungible and flexible than people

Where does that leave us? I think firmly in the second phase of the AI build-out. Real value is being built in the app layer (though how defensible it is…TBD).  

Trying to predict the next bottleneck, or whether Washington does this or that other thing wrt policy, or exactly how many data centers get built out…who can say? Certainly not me. It’s not the bet I’m trying to make 

I’m looking at who wins from rapidly improving intelligence available at increasingly cheaper prices, and critically, which leaders are able to move with conviction into this new operating paradigm

Commodities are getting hit pretty hard alongside the broader equity market as the surging U.S. dollar sucks liquidity out of the global financial system.  For those that follow me, I've been saying this from some time that there was risks if the dollar strengthens too quickly. 

The issue is that dollar-denominated debt becomes more expensive to service, financial conditions tighten, and investors are forced to raise cash, reduce leverage and sell assets. It becomes less about fundamentals and more about liquidity.

One thing I've learned over the years is that market leverage doesn't necessarily tell you when a correction will happen, but it tells you a great deal about how painful that correction could become. For some perspective, U.S. margin debt has surged to approximately $1.45 trillion, equivalent to roughly 58% of U.S. currency in circulation and 6.2% of M2 money supply. That's an extraordinary amount of leverage in the system, and when markets start moving against investors, it can accelerate the selling pressure.

Unfortunately, even gold isn't immune. During a liquidity-driven selloff, investors often sell what they can, not necessarily what they want to. Gold can become a source of cash to cover margin calls and offset losses elsewhere.

The irony is that the very forces driving the dollar higher could eventually create the conditions for its reversal. The U.S. government and broader financial system have become increasingly reliant on negative real interest rate

URANIUM'S BIGGEST PROBLEM: THE MINES THAT DON'T EXIST YET

Utilities are covered today. But who supplies their reactors in 2030, 2032 or 2035?

That's the tension in a December 2025 interview with Justin Huhn of Uranium Insider. The argument is even more relevant today.

In the 2000s uranium boom, spot went from below $10 to about $135/lb. Some mining shares rose 10- to 100-fold before crashing.

Huhn believes this cycle could last longer because uranium supply responds painfully slowly to higher prices.

A deposit cannot become a mine just because spot reaches $100. It needs permits, financing, infrastructure, construction and a successful ramp-up. That takes years.

Demand is more predictable. Reactors need refuelling, life extensions add consumption, and Japan is restarting units. China is building reactors, buying overseas uranium and expanding fuel services. Data centres add another reason to preserve nuclear power.

THE CONTRACTING CLOCK IS TICKING

Utilities are comfortable near term. Further out, the picture changes dramatically.

Sprott, citing U.S. EIA data, estimates maximum U.S. utility contract coverage falls from about 98% in 2026 to 60% in 2030 and just 9% by 2033.

That isn't a fuel-shortage forecast. Utilities can sign contracts and draw inventories.

But it means substantial demand remains unsecured, just as the market is counting on mines that have yet to produce a pound.

CAMECO IS SHOWING ITS HAND

Huhn's interview quoted $75/lb spot and $86/lb long-term. Those figures are dated.

On November 20, spot was around $90/lb. TradeTech's October long-term indicator hit $99/lb.

More revealing is what Cameco says about contracts.

In its Q3 2026 call, Cameco described market-linked floors in the mid-to-high $70s, ceilings reaching $160, and three-digit prices on fixed-price portions.

These are contract terms, not a guarantee of $160 realized prices. But they show how much bargaining power disciplined producers have gained.

Huhn argues new major mines need sustained higher prices, potentially north of $100/lb, to justify financing and execution risk.

A short spike won't build a mine. Sustained incentive pricing might.

THE MINES THAT MUST DELIVER

NexGen's Arrow study forecasts 28.8 million lb a year for its first five years. Enormous supply from one mine.

Since Huhn spoke, NexGen secured its construction licence in March 2026 and started construction in June.

But construction isn't production. Shaft sinking, ground conditions, commissioning and ramp-up still matter. NexGen's own capital-cost estimate has already risen from about C$1.3 billion in its 2021 study to C$2.2 billion in a 2024 update.

And Arrow is only one mine. Future supply depends on other projects delivering as promised.

If they slip, utilities can't order replacement pounds from mines that don't exist.

THE FINANCIAL WILDCARD

Huhn also explains the carry trade: when forward uranium prices sufficiently exceed spot, traders can buy uranium, store it and sell it for future delivery.

That can support spot buying before utilities need delivery. It is not a guaranteed price floor.

Physical trusts and speculative traders could amplify a rally. They could amplify the downside too.

MY JUDGMENT

Huhn sees opportunities in beaten-down small uranium stocks. Perhaps. But this is where I'd be selective.

A shortage doesn't make every deposit profitable. Higher uranium prices won't fix bad contracts, excessive capex, weak management or repeated dilution.

Some stocks gained 1,000% or more in the last bull market. Others never rewarded shareholders.

The opportunity isn't simply to own uranium in the ground.

It's to own companies that turn it into profitable pounds before shareholders run out of patience and money.

Buy when there is blood in the streets! 

Extreme fear is setting up the next leg higher

The S&P 500 has fallen 11.6% from its October high in seven straight sessions. Friday’s close sat 4.1 standard deviations below the 50-day average, the most oversold reading since August 2015. The Arms Index posted back-to-back capitulation readings. This is what extreme fear looks like, and extreme fear has historically marked buying opportunities, not the start of bear markets.

The market closed the week at 6,910, right on 6,900, the key Fibonacci support level of this year’s rally. Fast V-shaped recoveries form within days of capitulation, and corrections that hold support don’t become bear markets. From 6,900, the strongest past fast-V recoveries delivered 12-month gains of up to 38%, which puts 9,500 within reach. The timing adds to the case. 

The market is entering the sweet spot of the four-year presidential cycle, and the S&P has been higher a year after every midterm election since 1950.

Add a Fed pivot, and 10,000 is still in play. S&P 500 earnings will reach $450 in 2027, so the only argument is over the multiple. With the energy crisis passing, the 10-year Treasury yield will head to 4%, and the Greenspan Fed model then implies a multiple of 25. 

Even 22 times earnings gets the index to 10,000. Nothing has changed except the level of fear. There is no recession and no financial crisis, and investors will come to see AI not as a three-year buildout but as something like the railroads.

Fear flips to greed, as it did in 1998. After the Asian currency crisis and the Russia and LTCM shock, the S&P 500 fell 19% from its July peak. The Fed cut three times, the index regained its high by late November, and a year after the October low it was up 39%. When the Fed has eased after a no-recession sell-off, as in 1998, 2019 and 2025, the median 12-month gain has been 33.7%.

Many cite the 1990s to argue that the supply of AI capacity is outstripping demand. That’s wrong. The real lesson of the 1990s is the one Alan Greenspan drew: productivity gains let an economy run hot without stoking inflation. In 1995, after the Fed pivoted from hiking to easing with no recession, the S&P 500 gained 34.1%, the best pre-election year since 1950.

Leveraged products now amplify every swing between fear and greed, and this week’s selling was fear at full volume. The old saying is to buy when there is blood in the streets. Today there is no recession and no financial crisis, the energy shock is ending, and productivity and earnings are growing strongly. A Fed pivot is coming, and the market is cheap. 

That’s the time to buy.

Iranians are lining up for bread at 4 a.m., clutching cash and bank cards as fears of shortages and tighter access to subsidized bread deepen.

A circulating video shows a crowd pressing around a bakery before dawn, with captions saying people arrived early to buy bread before supplies ran out.

The scenes come amid reports of a quietly introduced “bread purchase management” system in Markazi, Khuzestan and Zanjan, with reports of expansion elsewhere and contradictory explanations from officials.

Under the reported rules, each person receives a monthly allowance equivalent to roughly 8 kilograms of subsidized flour, with purchases above that level charged at more than five times the subsidized rate.

That allowance works out to approximately 266 grams of flour per person a day, below the Health Ministry’s cited average consumption of roughly 333 grams.

Officials have disputed the “rationing” label, with some saying the changes target commercial purchases rather than ordinary households, but the opaque rollout has fueled confusion, queues and disputes at bakeries.

Even the hardline newspaper Kayhan criticized what it called the government’s “secret and suspicious implementation of bread rationing,” exposing concern within the system itself.

For households already struggling with soaring food prices and collapsing purchasing power, losing affordable access to bread means pressure on the most basic part of their diet.

🚨 UPDATE sur Riemann et elle est énorme 

Hier, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, annonçait avoir trouvé une preuve avec Claude. C'était une revendication, personne n'avait encore vérifié

Aujourd'hui, la Lean FRO et la Mathlib Initiative, les deux organisations derrière Lean et sa bibliothèque de maths, publient une déclaration commune : « We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct »

EN 24 HEURES !! 

Elles écrivent avoir « full confidence » dans la preuve et félicitent Alpöge

Après 167 ans cest le plus gros morceau des maths qui tombe, alors que tout le monde le voyait encore résister 30-50 ans. 

1. Ce qui a changé en 24h

Hier je vous disais que personne hors de son cercle n'avait confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

Les deux points sont réglés. Des dizaines de personnes ont recompilé la bibliothèque de leur côté et obtenu le même fichier de preuve, sans aucune erreur

Et l'énoncé démontré est bien celui de Mathlib, qui avait déjà été relu par des experts de Lean et de théorie des nombres

2. Comment ils ont vérifié

La preuve fait 17 millions de lignes de Lean et ne dépend directement que de Mathlib

La communauté a isolé l'énoncé de Riemann dans un fichier à part, qui n'importe que Mathlib, puis l'a comparé au théorème d'Alpöge avec deux outils indépendants, comparator et con-leche. Les deux confirment que c'est exactement le même énoncé

La preuve a ensuite été passée dans plusieurs vérificateurs, dont le noyau officiel de Lean, con-leche et con-ron, plus d'autres écrits par des tiers dans d'autres langages

Détail très fort : con-leche et con-ron ont eux-mêmes une preuve formelle qu'ils ne peuvent pas accepter une fausse preuve. Ça répond à la crainte d'une faille dans la logique de Lean que la preuve aurait pu exploiter

3. Claude des deux côtés

Andrew Sutherland, du MIT, publie tous ses fichiers de vérification. Et ses contrôles ont été lancés avec Claude Code

Sur sa page : les 175 187 modules compilent, la preuve n'utilise que les trois axiomes standard de Lean, et nanoda, un noyau indépendant écrit en Rust, accepte la preuve complète

Donc Claude a aidé à trouver la preuve, et Claude a aidé à la vérifier. Avec des outils indépendants à chaque étape. 

Pour le million du Clay Institute, les règles demandent une publication dans une revue reconnue, deux ans d'attente puis une acceptation générale par la communauté. Et Anthropic n'a fait aucune communication officielle

5. Ce que ça débloque

Comme je vous disait hier Des milliers de théorèmes commençaient par « si l'hypothèse de Riemann est vraie, alors… ». Ils tiennent maintenant sur une preuve vérifiée par machine

Pour les gros needs, Sutherland l'a déjà montré : en combinant la preuve avec une formalisation indépendante du critère de Robin, Lean démontre l'inégalité de Robin pour tout n > 5040, sans aucune mention de la fonction zêta

Le Lean blog conclut en attendant toute l'activité de la communauté pour expliquer les idées nouvelles de cette preuve. Les humains doivent maintenant comprendre ce que Claude et Alpöge ont trouvé, une première dans l’histoire 

L’ère de l’exponentielle vient de commencer, l’humanité entre dans un âge d’or

posts.text:
Watched 'Sirat' on @tylercowen's recommendation as best film of 2026.

It's spectacular. The amateur actors made me think of all the nomadic counterculture types I met backpacking around Europe in the 90s (now a bit old and grizzled and past their peak rave days, but still wandering).

The cinematography was a motion-picture landscape painting. 

The not-so-subtle political commentary on how these supposed bohemians are just obnoxious tourists somehow delusionally entering a conflict-zone the locals are trying to escape (and eventually paying for it).

The drug-fueled nihilism of it all, with human connection somehow surviving the LSD trips and endless hours inside rundown campers.

The easy manner they switch between French and Spanish until it becomes one patois, like anyone who's drifted between the two countries often. 

A bit long, but you have to settle into the rhythm of it. Unique film. 

Per the Quranic reference of the title, the supposed paradise they're seeking in the desert turns into hell very quickly. An American version of this would be some rah-rah Burning Man bore...the Euro version is a lot darker and more interesting.
